title: The Right Kind of Stubborn: persistence is attached to the goal, obstinacy to the method
summary: Graham argues persistence and obstinacy are different behaviors, not labels applied after the fact. The persistent are attached to the goal and open to disagreement; the obstinate cling to their first ideas. Persistence is built from five qualities: energy, imagination, resilience, good judgement, and a focus on a goal.

principles.text: Be attached to the goal, not to your ideas about how to reach it.
principles.quote: The persistent are attached to the goal. The obstinate are attached to their ideas about how to reach it.

principles.text: Seek out disagreement: the persistent get more engaged when you point out problems.
principles.quote: They're never _more_ engaged than when you disagree with them. Whereas the obstinate don't want to hear you.

principles.text: Persistence needs imagination: to keep trying things, you must keep thinking of things to try.
principles.quote: Which means the persistent must also be imaginative. To keep trying things, you have to keep thinking of things to try.

principles.text: Resilience means setbacks can't change your morale, but they can change your mind.
principles.quote: Resilience means setbacks can't change your morale, not that they can't change your mind.

principles.text: Judge by expected value and give way on low-level details, while holding firm on the goal chosen higher up.
principles.quote: You'll give way on any point low down in the decision tree, if its expected value drops sufficiently, but energy and resilience keep pushing you toward whatever you chose higher up.

principles.text: Make the goal specific enough to guide action; start small and expand once moving.
principles.quote: Start by erring on the small side. If you're inexperienced you'll inevitably err on one side or the other, and if you err on the side of making the goal too broad, you won't get anywhere.
